subject: AR terms for unbalanced panel data

messages.author: 930400b04e8b7ce6
messages.subject: AR terms for unbalanced panel data
parts:
Hello all,

I'm fitting an AR(p) model on unbalanced panel data, where some individuals may be observed only once and some have up to 20 observations. 

My question is: when using AR models in INLA, I am curious how having different # of observations for individuals is handled - if I fit an AR(3) model and yet many individuals have only 1 observation, what happens/ how is this handled internally? 

Thank you,
Kyle

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] AR terms for unbalanced panel data
parts:
Can you clarify more precisely how you’re defining the model?
If it’s a joint AR model for all individuals, you’ll simply have more information for time point with more observations.
If it’s and AR model that’s replicated iid across individuals, then it will rely on there being enough individuals with information about the ar parameters; if it’s able to estimate the ar parameters with only those individuals included, then it should in principle handle having the sparsely observed individuals as well; it will in effect do prediction/reconstruction for all unobserved time points.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] AR terms for unbalanced panel data
parts:
example, with person.1 being observed at time 1,2,4,4, (yes, twice at
time 4),and person.2 being observed at time 2,3,5, then

idx=c(1,2,4,4,2,3,5)
r=c(1,1,1,1,2,2,2)
values=1:5

and you use

f(idx, model="ar1", replicate=r, values=values)

its important to give 'values' which are 1:n for which n is the max time
for the AR1 to be observed or you want it to exists.

to experiment with this, you can fix the observational noise with

family="gaussian",
control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(PREC),
fixed=TRUE))))

where PREC=1/VAR, like exp(14) if you have 'exact' observations.

with few observations it can be a little tricky to balance noise
observations and the properties of the AR1, as you have multiple
interpretations of the data.

The AR model is defined to be stationary, i.e. at time 1 it has the
stationary distribution, so it's not "free". The inla.doc("ar") ar.pdf
documentation says "the joint distribution for {xt , t = 1, . . . ,
p}, is
set to the stationary distribution for the process, hence there are no
boundary issues".

Also, when you have an ar model with replicates, the time points are
the same for all individuals, i.e. you need
values=seq_len(maximum_time_lag)
to ensure all time points are included, like Haavard stated.

(To have different time intervals for different individuals, you would
need to build a bespoke model with "rgeneric". If the time intervals
are similar in length, it's much easier to use the built-in
"replicated ar" approach.)

What is the setting under which you "train" and "test"? Under a model
where the AR model is directly observed, plus measurement noise,
predictions for new individuals would have variance s^2 (where s is
the estimated AR model standard deviation) whereas predictions for
observed time points of an individual in the training set would have
variance
around 1/(1/s^2+1/s_obs^2), where s_obs is the observation standard
deviation, which is smaller than both s^2 and s_obs^2. For temporal
interpolation the variance will be somewhere between those two
prediction variances.
It's not clear to me what type of "overfitting" you are referring to?

Finn

parts:
Hi,

this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
the best it can at computing information about the posterior
distributions for the specified model.

It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
the latent variables of the defined model.
Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
intercept.
Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.

Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
time t_i and individual j_i:
\eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
The observed values are
y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).

The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
x-values for observed times&individuals)
The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
for the x_{t,j} values.

The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
all have been observed.
If you plot the posterior std.dev values for all t=1,...,T for a
single individual, you should see small values for times associated
with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
unobserved, time points.
If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
observed time points would be on the order of
1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
(not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
\sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,

For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
(you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
are.

I'm not sure if this answers your question...

Finn

Hi,

this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
the best it can at computing information about the posterior
distributions for the specified model.

It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
the latent variables of the defined model.
Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
intercept.
Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.

Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
time t_i and individual j_i:
\eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
The observed values are
y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).

The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
x-values for observed times&individuals)
The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
for the x_{t,j} values.

The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
all have been observed.
If you plot the posterior std.dev values for all t=1,...,T for a
single individual, you should see small values for times associated
with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
unobserved, time points.
If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
observed time points would be on the order of
1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
(not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
\sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,

For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
(you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
are.

I'm not sure if this answers your question...

Hi,

this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
the best it can at computing information about the posterior
distributions for the specified model.

It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
the latent variables of the defined model.
Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
intercept.
Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.

Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
time t_i and individual j_i:
\eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
The observed values are
y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).

The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
x-values for observed times&individuals)
The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
for the x_{t,j} values.

The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
all have been observed.
If you plot the posterior std.dev values for all t=1,...,T for a
single individual, you should see small values for times associated
with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
unobserved, time points.
If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
observed time points would be on the order of
1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
(not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
\sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,

For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
(you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
are.

I'm not sure if this answers your question...

Finn

Hi,

this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
the best it can at computing information about the posterior
distributions for the specified model.

It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
the latent variables of the defined model.
Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
intercept.
Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.

Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
time t_i and individual j_i:
\eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
The observed values are
y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).

The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
x-values for observed times&individuals)
The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
for the x_{t,j} values.

The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
all have been observed.
If you plot the posterior std.dev values for all t=1,...,T for a
single individual, you should see small values for times associated
with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
unobserved, time points.
If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
observed time points would be on the order of
1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
(not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
\sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,

For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
(you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
are.

I'm not sure if this answers your question...

Finn

On Thursday, August 18, 2022 at 8:50:06 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:

The AR model is defined to be stationary, i.e. at time 1 it has the
stationary distribution, so it's not "free". The inla.doc("ar") ar.pdf
documentation says "the joint distribution for {xt , t = 1, . . . ,
p}, is
set to the stationary distribution for the process, hence there are no
boundary issues".

Also, when you have an ar model with replicates, the time points are
the same for all individuals, i.e. you need
values=seq_len(maximum_time_lag)
to ensure all time points are included, like Haavard stated.

(To have different time intervals for different individuals, you would
need to build a bespoke model with "rgeneric". If the time intervals
are similar in length, it's much easier to use the built-in
"replicated ar" approach.)

What is the setting under which you "train" and "test"? Under a model
where the AR model is directly observed, plus measurement noise,
predictions for new individuals would have variance s^2 (where s is
the estimated AR model standard deviation) whereas predictions for
observed time points of an individual in the training set would have
variance
around 1/(1/s^2+1/s_obs^2), where s_obs is the observation standard
deviation, which is smaller than both s^2 and s_obs^2. For temporal
interpolation the variance will be somewhere between those two
prediction variances.
It's not clear to me what type of "overfitting" you are referring to?

Finn

I create indices like so:

df = df %>% group_by(ID) %>% mutate(index = rank(date_f))

The result is an individual's first observation is given by index == 1 and they increment by 1 every observation. Residuals are just `model$summary.fitted.values$mean - df$target`. One interesting thing is that changing the prior seems to alleviate the issue.

The questionable prior is `hyper_fixed = list(theta1=list(initial=0.5, fixed=T))` while `hyper_AR_f  = list(theta1 = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(3 * target_ln_sd, 0.01)), theta2 = list(prior="pc.cor1", param=c(0.9, 0.9)))`
